# Existence and Uniqueness of Direct Limit of a Sequence of Groups — Lemma 3

## 0. The setting

The statement to be proved lives inside the standard construction of the direct limit of a
sequence (direct system indexed by $\mathbb{N}$) of groups. We record that construction in
full, so that the proof below is self-contained.

**Data.**

* A sequence of groups $\sequence{G_n}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ (we take $\mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$;
  nothing depends on where the indexing starts).
* For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$ a group homomorphism $f_n : G_n \to G_{n+1}$.

**Composite maps.** For $m \le p$ in $\mathbb{N}$ define $f_{m,p} : G_m \to G_p$ by
$$
f_{m,m} := \operatorname{id}_{G_m}, \qquad f_{m,p+1} := f_p \circ f_{m,p} \quad (p \ge m).
$$
Thus $f_{m,p} = f_{p-1} \circ f_{p-2} \circ \cdots \circ f_m$ for $m < p$. Being a composite of
homomorphisms (and the identity being a homomorphism), each $f_{m,p}$ is a group homomorphism.

**Lemma 0 (transitivity of the composites).** For all $m \le n \le p$,
$$
f_{n,p} \circ f_{m,n} = f_{m,p}.
$$

*Proof.* Fix $m \le n$ and induct on $p \ge n$.

*Base $p = n$:* $f_{n,n} \circ f_{m,n} = \operatorname{id}_{G_n} \circ f_{m,n} = f_{m,n}$.

*Induction step:* assume $f_{n,p} \circ f_{m,n} = f_{m,p}$ for some $p \ge n$. Then, using the
recursive definition twice,
$$
f_{n,p+1} \circ f_{m,n} = (f_p \circ f_{n,p}) \circ f_{m,n} = f_p \circ (f_{n,p} \circ f_{m,n})
 = f_p \circ f_{m,p} = f_{m,p+1}.
$$
$\Box$

**The underlying set.** Let
$$
X := \set{\tuple{x,n} : n \in \mathbb{N},\ x \in G_n}
$$
be the disjoint union of the $G_n$, and define a relation $\sim$ on $X$ by
$$
\tuple{x,m} \sim \tuple{y,n}
\quad :\Longleftrightarrow \quad
\exists\, p \ge \max \set{m,n} : \ \map {f_{m,p}} x = \map {f_{n,p}} y .
$$
By **Lemma 1** of the construction (reproved as Proposition A.1 in the Appendix below), $\sim$ is
an equivalence relation on $X$. Write $\eqclass {\tuple{x,n}} {}$ for the $\sim$-class of
$\tuple{x,n}$ and put
$$
G_\infty := X / \sim .
$$

**The group structure.** By **Lemma 2** of the construction (reproved as Proposition A.2 in the
Appendix below), the prescription
$$
\eqclass {\tuple{x,m}} {} \cdot \eqclass {\tuple{y,n}} {}
 := \eqclass {\tuple{\map{f_{m,p}}x \, \map{f_{n,p}}y,\ p}} {},
 \qquad \text{any } p \ge \max\set{m,n},
$$
is independent of the choice of $p$ and of the chosen representatives, and makes $G_\infty$ a
group. (The product $\map{f_{m,p}}x \, \map{f_{n,p}}y$ is formed in the group $G_p$, which makes
sense precisely because $p \ge m$ and $p \ge n$.) The canonical maps are
$\map {\iota_n} x := \eqclass {\tuple{x,n}} {}$.

**Hypothesis for Lemma 3 (the compatible cocone).** Let $H$ be a group and let
$h_n : G_n \to H$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$, be group homomorphisms which are *compatible* with the
system, i.e.
$$
h_{n+1} \circ f_n = h_n \qquad \text{for every } n \in \mathbb{N}. \tag{C}
$$

**Lemma 3 (to be proved).** The assignment
$$
h_\infty : G_\infty \to H, \qquad \eqclass {\tuple{x_n,n}} {} \mapsto \map {h_n} {x_n}
$$
is a well-defined group homomorphism.

---

## 1. Step 1: compatibility with all composites

**Claim 1.** For all $m \le p$ in $\mathbb{N}$,
$$
h_p \circ f_{m,p} = h_m .
$$

*Proof.* Fix $m$ and induct on $p \ge m$.

*Base $p = m$:* $h_m \circ f_{m,m} = h_m \circ \operatorname{id}_{G_m} = h_m$.

*Induction step:* suppose $h_p \circ f_{m,p} = h_m$ for some $p \ge m$. Then
$$
h_{p+1} \circ f_{m,p+1}
 = h_{p+1} \circ \paren{f_p \circ f_{m,p}}
 = \paren{h_{p+1} \circ f_p} \circ f_{m,p}
 \overset{(C)}{=} h_p \circ f_{m,p}
 = h_m .
$$
By induction the claim holds for every $p \ge m$. $\blacksquare$

Explicitly: $\map {h_p} {\map {f_{m,p}} x} = \map {h_m} x$ for every $x \in G_m$ and every
$p \ge m$.

## 2. Step 2: $h_\infty$ is well-defined

A map out of a quotient set $X/\sim$ given by a formula on representatives is well-defined
exactly when (i) the formula assigns a value to *every* element of $X$, and (ii) $\sim$-equivalent
elements of $X$ receive the same value. (Then the induced assignment on classes is a genuine
function: it is total because every class is non-empty, and single-valued by (ii).)

(i) Every element of $X$ is of the form $\tuple{x,n}$ with $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $x \in G_n$, and
$\map {h_n} x \in H$ is defined, since $h_n : G_n \to H$ is a mapping. So the formula
$\tuple{x,n} \mapsto \map {h_n} x$ defines a mapping $\widetilde h : X \to H$.

(ii) Let $\tuple{x,m} \sim \tuple{y,n}$. By definition of $\sim$ there is some
$p \ge \max\set{m,n}$ with
$$
\map {f_{m,p}} x = \map {f_{n,p}} y \qquad \text{in } G_p .
$$
Applying the mapping $h_p$ to both sides of this equation and using Claim 1 twice (once with the
pair $m \le p$, once with the pair $n \le p$):
$$
\map {h_m} x
 = \map {h_p} {\map {f_{m,p}} x}
 = \map {h_p} {\map {f_{n,p}} y}
 = \map {h_n} y .
$$
Hence $\widetilde h$ is constant on $\sim$-classes.

Therefore there is a unique mapping $h_\infty : G_\infty \to H$ with
$h_\infty \circ \pi = \widetilde h$, where $\pi : X \to G_\infty$ is the quotient map; concretely,
$$
\map {h_\infty} {\eqclass {\tuple{x,n}} {}} = \map {h_n} x
$$
for *every* representative $\tuple{x,n}$ of the class, which is precisely the asserted formula.
So $h_\infty$ is a well-defined mapping. $\blacksquare$

## 3. Step 3: $h_\infty$ is a group homomorphism

Let $a, b \in G_\infty$ be arbitrary. Choose representatives: $a = \eqclass {\tuple{x,m}} {}$ and
$b = \eqclass {\tuple{y,n}} {}$ with $x \in G_m$, $y \in G_n$ (possible since $\pi$ is surjective).
Put $p := \max \set{m,n}$, so $p \ge m$ and $p \ge n$.

By the definition of the group operation on $G_\infty$,
$$
a \, b = \eqclass {\tuple{\map{f_{m,p}}x \, \map{f_{n,p}}y,\ p}} {} .
$$
Since $h_\infty$ is well-defined (Step 2), we may compute its value on this class using this very
representative:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\map {h_\infty} {a b}
&= \map {h_p} {\map{f_{m,p}}x \, \map{f_{n,p}}y} \\
&= \map {h_p} {\map{f_{m,p}}x} \cdot \map {h_p} {\map{f_{n,p}}y}
   && \text{($h_p$ is a homomorphism $G_p \to H$)} \\
&= \map {h_m} x \cdot \map {h_n} y
   && \text{(Claim 1, applied to $m \le p$ and to $n \le p$)} \\
&= \map {h_\infty} a \cdot \map {h_\infty} b
   && \text{(definition of $h_\infty$ on the chosen representatives).}
\end{aligned}
$$
As $a, b \in G_\infty$ were arbitrary, $h_\infty$ is a group homomorphism. $\blacksquare$

Consequently $h_\infty$ automatically satisfies $\map {h_\infty} {e_{G_\infty}} = e_H$ and
$\map {h_\infty} {a^{-1}} = \map {h_\infty} a ^{-1}$, as every group homomorphism does.

**Remark (the hypotheses actually used).** The proof used exactly three things: that each $h_n$
is a homomorphism $G_n \to H$; the compatibility (C); and the two defining formulas (for $\sim$
and for the product on $G_\infty$). Compatibility is not merely convenient but necessary: taking
$x \in G_n$ we have $\tuple{x,n} \sim \tuple{\map {f_n} x, n+1}$ (witness $p = n+1$), so any
well-defined $h_\infty$ satisfying the displayed formula forces
$\map {h_n} x = \map {h_{n+1}} {\map {f_n} x}$, i.e. (C).

## 4. Remark: $h_\infty$ is the unique map with $h_\infty \circ \iota_n = h_n$

For $x \in G_n$ we have $\map {h_\infty} {\map {\iota_n} x} = \map {h_\infty} {\eqclass {\tuple{x,n}} {}}
= \map {h_n} x$, i.e. $h_\infty \circ \iota_n = h_n$ for all $n$. Moreover, if
$g : G_\infty \to H$ is any mapping with $g \circ \iota_n = h_n$ for all $n$, then for any
$a \in G_\infty$, writing $a = \eqclass {\tuple{x,n}} {} = \map {\iota_n} x$ we get
$\map g a = \map {h_n} x = \map {h_\infty} a$; hence $g = h_\infty$. (This is the part of the
universal property that Lemma 3 feeds into; it is not needed for the statement itself.)

---

## Appendix: the two facts about $G_\infty$ that were used

For completeness we prove the two assertions about the ambient construction quoted above
(Lemmas 1 and 2 of the construction), namely that $\sim$ is an equivalence relation and that the
operation on $G_\infty$ is well-defined and makes $G_\infty$ a group. Only Lemma 0, the definition
of $\sim$ and the definition of the operation are used; nothing in the Appendix depends on
Sections 1–3.

**Proposition A.1.** $\sim$ is an equivalence relation on $X$.

*Proof.* *Reflexivity:* for $\tuple{x,m} \in X$ take $p = m \ge \max\set{m,m}$; then
$\map {f_{m,m}} x = x = \map {f_{m,m}} x$.

*Symmetry:* immediate, since the defining condition is symmetric in $\tuple{x,m}$ and
$\tuple{y,n}$.

*Transitivity:* suppose $\tuple{x,m} \sim \tuple{y,n}$ and $\tuple{y,n} \sim \tuple{z,k}$, witnessed
by $p \ge \max\set{m,n}$ with $\map {f_{m,p}} x = \map {f_{n,p}} y$ and by
$q \ge \max\set{n,k}$ with $\map {f_{n,q}} y = \map {f_{k,q}} z$. Put $r := \max\set{p,q}$; then
$r \ge p \ge m$, $r \ge n$, and $r \ge q \ge k$. Using Lemma 0 repeatedly,
$$
\map {f_{m,r}} x = \map {f_{p,r}} {\map {f_{m,p}} x} = \map {f_{p,r}} {\map {f_{n,p}} y}
 = \map {f_{n,r}} y,
$$
$$
\map {f_{k,r}} z = \map {f_{q,r}} {\map {f_{k,q}} z} = \map {f_{q,r}} {\map {f_{n,q}} y}
 = \map {f_{n,r}} y .
$$
Hence $\map {f_{m,r}} x = \map {f_{k,r}} z$ with $r \ge \max\set{m,k}$, i.e.
$\tuple{x,m} \sim \tuple{z,k}$. $\Box$

**Proposition A.2.** The operation
$\eqclass {\tuple{x,m}} {} \cdot \eqclass {\tuple{y,n}} {}
:= \eqclass {\tuple{\map{f_{m,p}}x \, \map{f_{n,p}}y,\ p}} {}$
is independent of the choice of $p \ge \max\set{m,n}$ and of the representatives, and it makes
$G_\infty$ a group.

*Proof.* *A key identity.* For $m \le p \le r$ and $n \le p \le r$ we have, since $f_{p,r}$ is a
homomorphism and by Lemma 0,
$$
\map {f_{p,r}} {\map{f_{m,p}}x \, \map{f_{n,p}}y}
 = \map {f_{p,r}} {\map{f_{m,p}}x} \, \map {f_{p,r}} {\map{f_{n,p}}y}
 = \map{f_{m,r}}x \, \map{f_{n,r}}y . \tag{$*$}
$$
In particular $\tuple{\map{f_{m,p}}x \, \map{f_{n,p}}y,\ p} \sim
\tuple{\map{f_{m,r}}x \, \map{f_{n,r}}y,\ r}$.

*Independence of $p$.* If $p, p' \ge \max\set{m,n}$, put $r := \max\set{p,p'}$; by ($*$) both
$\tuple{\map{f_{m,p}}x \, \map{f_{n,p}}y, p}$ and
$\tuple{\map{f_{m,p'}}x \, \map{f_{n,p'}}y, p'}$ are $\sim$-equivalent to
$\tuple{\map{f_{m,r}}x \, \map{f_{n,r}}y, r}$, hence to each other.

*Independence of representatives.* Let $\tuple{x,m} \sim \tuple{x',m'}$, witnessed by
$s \ge \max\set{m,m'}$ with $\map {f_{m,s}} x = \map {f_{m',s}} {x'}$, and
$\tuple{y,n} \sim \tuple{y',n'}$, witnessed by $t \ge \max\set{n,n'}$ with
$\map {f_{n,t}} y = \map {f_{n',t}} {y'}$. Put $r := \max\set{s,t}$; then $r$ dominates each of
$m,m',n,n'$. By Lemma 0,
$$
\map {f_{m,r}} x = \map {f_{s,r}} {\map {f_{m,s}} x} = \map {f_{s,r}} {\map {f_{m',s}} {x'}}
 = \map {f_{m',r}} {x'},
$$
and likewise $\map {f_{n,r}} y = \map {f_{n',r}} {y'}$. Hence
$$
\map{f_{m,r}}x \, \map{f_{n,r}}y = \map{f_{m',r}}{x'} \, \map{f_{n',r}}{y'}
$$
as elements of $G_r$, so the two candidate products, computed with the admissible index $r$ in
both cases, are literally the same class. Combined with the independence of $p$ just proved, the
operation is well-defined on $G_\infty \times G_\infty$.

*Group axioms.* Let $a = \eqclass {\tuple{x,m}} {}$, $b = \eqclass {\tuple{y,n}} {}$,
$c = \eqclass {\tuple{z,k}} {}$ and fix an index $r \ge \max\set{m,n,k}$. Write
$\bar x := \map {f_{m,r}} x$, $\bar y := \map {f_{n,r}} y$, $\bar z := \map {f_{k,r}} z$, all in
$G_r$; note $a = \eqclass {\tuple{\bar x, r}} {}$, $b = \eqclass {\tuple{\bar y, r}} {}$,
$c = \eqclass {\tuple{\bar z, r}} {}$, because e.g. $\map {f_{m,r}} x = \map {f_{r,r}} {\bar x}$
exhibits $r$ as a witness for $\tuple{x,m} \sim \tuple{\bar x, r}$. Since $r$ is an admissible
index for any two of these representatives and $f_{r,r} = \operatorname{id}_{G_r}$, the definition
of the operation (evaluated at the index $r$, which is legitimate by the independence of $p$
proved above) reads simply
$$
\eqclass {\tuple{u, r}} {} \cdot \eqclass {\tuple{v, r}} {}
 = \eqclass {\tuple{\map {f_{r,r}} u \, \map {f_{r,r}} v,\ r}} {}
 = \eqclass {\tuple{uv, r}} {}
\qquad (u, v \in G_r). \tag{$**$}
$$
Applying ($**$) twice,
$$
(ab)c = \eqclass {\tuple{\bar x \bar y, r}} {} \cdot \eqclass {\tuple{\bar z, r}} {}
 = \eqclass {\tuple{(\bar x \bar y) \bar z, r}} {}
 = \eqclass {\tuple{\bar x (\bar y \bar z), r}} {}
 = \eqclass {\tuple{\bar x, r}} {} \cdot \eqclass {\tuple{\bar y \bar z, r}} {} = a(bc),
$$
the middle equality being associativity in the group $G_r$. Hence the operation is associative.

Next, all the elements $\tuple{e_{G_n}, n}$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$, are $\sim$-equivalent: for
$n \le p$ we have $\map {f_{n,p}} {e_{G_n}} = e_{G_p}$ because $f_{n,p}$ is a homomorphism, so
$p := \max \set{n, n'}$ witnesses $\tuple{e_{G_n}, n} \sim \tuple{e_{G_{n'}}, n'}$. Let
$\varepsilon$ denote their common class. For $a = \eqclass {\tuple{x,m}} {}$, using the
representatives $\tuple{x,m}$ and $\tuple{e_{G_m}, m}$ and ($**$) with $r$ replaced by $m$,
$$
a \varepsilon = \eqclass {\tuple{x \, e_{G_m}, m}} {} = \eqclass {\tuple{x, m}} {} = a,
\qquad
\varepsilon a = \eqclass {\tuple{e_{G_m} \, x, m}} {} = a .
$$
Finally, again by ($**$) at the index $m$,
$$
\eqclass {\tuple{x,m}} {} \cdot \eqclass {\tuple{x^{-1},m}} {}
 = \eqclass {\tuple{x x^{-1}, m}} {} = \eqclass {\tuple{e_{G_m}, m}} {} = \varepsilon,
$$
and symmetrically $\eqclass {\tuple{x^{-1},m}} {} \cdot \eqclass {\tuple{x,m}} {} = \varepsilon$,
so every element of $G_\infty$ has an inverse. Thus $G_\infty$ is a group. $\Box$

$\blacksquare$
